title: The sky is the platter
hook: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls: creation performs the aarti (Dhanasri M1, ang 13)
carry: you don't light it, you notice it

segments.voice: Yesterday, gagan, the sky; your line was gagan mai thaal. Today, what the platter is for.
screen: `GAGAN MAI THAAL — THE SKY, A PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Evening at a Hindu temple. The bells start. A priest lifts a brass tray of small flames and moves it in slow circles before the image of the deity. Incense curls up. Someone waves a fan of white hair. Flowers lie heaped at the front. People sing, clap, reach toward the flames and draw the warmth back over their eyes. That's an aarti. Sohila's third hymn takes the items on that tray and finds each one, much larger, somewhere in the world.
screen: `A BRASS TRAY OF FLAMES.` → `INCENSE, A FAN, FLOWERS.` → `EVERY ITEM, FOUND IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Aarti is the waving of lamps, a way of honoring what is dear by circling light before it. Now walk through the hymn with the tray in mind. The platter: the sky. The lamps: the sun and the moon. Then: taarika mandal janak moti, the circles of stars are like pearls scattered across it. More items follow, the incense, the fan, the flowers; we'll take those tomorrow. Then the refrain. In paraphrase: what a wonderful aarti this is, O Destroyer of fear; this is Your aarti. And the unstruck sound, the music no hand plays, sounds like the temple drums. So who is performing the aarti? Not a priest. Creation itself. In the hymn, the whole universe, every evening, lifts its lamps toward the One. In Sikh practice the hymn itself is sung as the aarti, with no tray and no flames: the sound is the offering. A few historic gurdwaras also keep an evening ceremony with lamps alongside the singing, and Sikhs differ on that practice. Both share the line's big picture: the offering is already happening, all around, all the time. You don't light it. You notice it.
screen: `AARTI: CIRCLING LIGHT IN HONOR.` · `SKY, SUN AND MOON, STARS AS PEARLS.` · `WHAT A WONDERFUL AARTI THIS IS.` · `CREATION ITSELF IS OFFERING.` · then, large: `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.`

segments.voice: Find the sky, through a window or outside: the moon, one star, the orange glow of a city night, or the daytime blue as it is. Picture it as a tray held up in honor, and yourself at the edge of the crowd beneath it. If you pray, say Waheguru once.
Aarti. The offering of circling lamps; in Sohila's third hymn, the aarti the whole creation performs, with the sky as its platter.
Your line: you don't light it, you notice it. The offering is already going on. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite this hymn nightly within Kirtan Sohila, and gurdwaras also sing it on its own in the evening as the Aarti, usually without lamps, while a few historic gurdwaras also keep a lamp ceremony.
